analysis.one_liner: Strips EPA authority to regulate greenhouse gases and voids its power-plant carbon rules.
analysis.headline: Backed by 152 House Republicans, the bill died in committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites the Clean Air Act to say carbon dioxide, methane, and other greenhouse gases are not air pollutants, and declares that no federal law authorizes regulating climate change. It voids the EPA's proposed rules limiting carbon emissions from new and existing power plants, and blocks any future EPA rule that the agency finds would cost jobs unless Congress and the President approve it.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners, coal-burning utilities, and other carbon-intensive industries gain by shedding the federal rules that would have required them to cut greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.

how_it_helps.text: Removes greenhouse gases from the definition of 'air pollutant' under the Clean Air Act, ending the legal basis for federal carbon regulation.
Declares the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, and the Solid Waste Disposal Act do not authorize or require regulation of climate change.
Voids the EPA's proposed rules limiting carbon emissions from new and existing electric utility generating units, and any similar successor rules.

Requires an employment analysis before any EPA rule and bars any rule found to have a negative impact on employment from taking effect without approval from Congress and the President — a standing veto over EPA regulation.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the cost of increased climate change and unregulated air pollution, including the health effects of power-plant emissions that no other federal rule would address.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to climate and air pollution

drawbacks.text: By declaring that no federal law regulates climate change, the bill removes the entire federal backstop on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, the largest source of US carbon pollution.

The employment test in Section 4 is one-sided: any EPA rule found to cost jobs — even one whose health and climate benefits exceed its costs — could not take effect without new acts of Congress, a hurdle few rules would clear.

The strongest good-faith objection acknowledged by supporters: climate and power-plant rules impose real compliance costs that can raise electricity prices and eliminate jobs in coal-dependent communities, which is why the bill requires an employment analysis and a jobs-impact test before rules take effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives carbon-intensive industries relief from regulation at a cost borne broadly by the public in climate and air-pollution harms. Its jobs provision gives workers a safeguard in name, but because it blocks any rule with a job loss anywhere in the economy, it functions as a near-blanket prohibition on new EPA regulation rather than a balanced test.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four different House committees, then to a subcommittee, and none of them ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gary Palmer introduced the bill on November 3, 2015, with 101 original cosponsors joining on introduction.

It was referred to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Agriculture — a split referral that gave each panel jurisdiction only over the pieces under its purview.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment.
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
152 House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mining, coal-fired utilities, and other carbon-intensive industries are better off: the EPA's power-plant carbon rules remained subject to court challenge but were never voided by this bill, and no other carbon legislation moved either. People who rely on federal air-pollution protections are no worse off than before, since nothing changed.

for.name: Rep. Gary Palmer
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and recruited 101 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 152 of 247 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-Republican backing without any Democratic support.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Made the EPA's power-plant carbon rules (the Clean Power Plan) a signature priority of his administration, putting the White House squarely against any legislation voiding them.

sides.party_line_note: All 152 cosponsors were Republicans and none of the chamber's Democrats signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists.

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired power plants
industries.note: The bill voids the EPA's carbon rules for electric generating units, the regulations that hit coal-burning plants hardest, sparing the industry large compliance costs while leaving power-plant emissions unregulated. Its gain comes at the public's expense in climate and air-pollution harms.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and other greenhouse-gas emitters
industries.note: Removing methane, nitrous oxide, HFCs, PFCs, and sulfur hexafluoride from the Clean Air Act ends the legal basis for regulating those emissions, including methane leaks from oil and gas operations.
Fossil-fuel utilities avoid compliance costs, while utilities that had invested in cleaner generation or planned for the proposed carbon rules lose the regulatory certainty those rules provided.
Voiding the power-plant carbon rules removes the demand signal for renewable generation and pollution-control equipment that the rules would have driven.
